transfer.title: Transfer case · the textbook's traffic management system
transfer.text: The textbook's traffic management system has a control process that polls separate sensor processes and traffic-light control processes. One sensor process stops replying. This is a different system from the booking service.
transfer.source: Source slides 31–32 (master–slave architectures and the traffic management example)
transfer.question: In this pattern, which process must detect the missing reply, and why?
transfer.answer: The master. In the master–slave pattern the master computes, coordinates and communicates, and it controls the slaves. The slave processes only acquire data or drive equipment, so they cannot judge the whole system.

X01.commonError: Students call an app “local” because it runs on the phone. Ask what happens to it when the network is down.

X02.answerKey: hide distribution only when the delay does not change what users should do
X02.commonError: Students want full transparency. Ask what a user should do during a pending remote operation if nothing shows it is pending.

SCALE.answerKey: the serialized database stays the bottleneck
SCALE.commonError: Students add servers for every slowdown. Ask which resource is constrained and whether the work can run in parallel.

X02A.concept: what a lost response leaves unknown
X02A.answerKey: whether the operation executed or committed
X02A.commonError: Students equate a timeout with failure. Draw the three histories that fit one lost response.

X03.answerKey: a queue does not prevent duplicate effects
X03.commonError: Students believe a message queue delivers exactly once. Ask what happens when the receiver crashes after acting but before acknowledging.

CHECK1.answerKey: a status query or durable record by operation identity
CHECK1.commonError: Students write “the server did nothing” after a timeout. Make them narrow the claim to “no response arrived in time”.

X04.answerKey: the meaning of values, operations and errors
X04.commonError: Students expect middleware to settle compatibility. Representation conversion does not agree what the data means.

X05.commonError: Students equate four layers with four machines. Layers are responsibilities; tiers are where they run.
X05.answerKey2: layers are logical; tiers are deployment
X05.question: Can client and server processes run on the same computer?
X05.answer: Yes. The logical interaction model is distinct from deployment across machines.
X05.question2: Why is a four-layer design not automatically a four-tier deployment?
X05.answer2: Layers are logical responsibilities. Several layers may share one process or computer. Tiers describe deployment boundaries.

X06.commonError: Students pick one pattern as the universal answer. Ask which non-functional requirement decided it.

lists.title: Architectural patterns
items: Master–slave: real-time systems that need guaranteed interaction response times
Two-tier client–server: simple systems, or systems centralised for security reasons
Multi-tier client–server: a high volume of transactions processed by the server
Distributed component: resources from different systems and databases must be combined
Peer-to-peer: computation or information exchange across many nodes without central control

CHECK2.answerKey: who detects failure and what is retried
CHECK2.commonError: Students add boxes instead of responsibilities. Ask who detects failure, who retries and who reconciles duplicates.

B01.answerKey: coordination and failure-handling costs can exceed the benefit
B01.commonError: Students assume more distributed is always better. Ask what the extra coordination costs for a simple application.

X07.answerKey: unreliable connectivity favours local processing, with synchronisation designed
X07.commonError: Students choose a fat client for speed and forget synchronisation. Ask how conflicts and stale data are handled.

lists.title: Two-tier client–server architectures
items: A single logical server plus an indefinite number of clients that use it
Thin-client model: the presentation layer runs on the client; data management, application processing and the database run on the server
Fat-client model: some or all application processing runs on the client; data management and the database stay on the server

X09.answerKey: configuration, integration and change impacts remain
X09.commonError: Students think a subscription removes engineering. List what still needs design: configuration, access control, data handling, change impact.

lists.title: Software as a service
items: Hosting the software remotely and providing access over the Internet
Deployed on one or more servers and accessed through a web browser, not installed locally
Owned and managed by a software provider, not by the organisations using it
Paid for by usage or by subscription

X10.answerKey: a delivery model versus an internal organisation
X10.commonError: Students use SaaS and SOA as synonyms. One says how the software is supplied; the other says how it is built.

AISYS.concept: retry safety with an external AI effect
AISYS.answerKey: check the key before any external effect; do not re-ask the model
AISYS.commonError: Students retry the AI call to “confirm” the first one. A retry is a new request; a model may answer it differently.
AISYS.answer: Before any external effect. The service records the key with the committed operation and its outcome. A retry with the same key returns that stored outcome instead of executing again. Calling the AI service again cannot confirm what happened the first time. It is a new request. A non-deterministic model may produce a different draft, so repeating it creates a second, different effect. Time out the AI call with a defined action. Never let model output trigger an effect that has not been recorded against the key.

APPLY.answerKey: send only the recorded message; never re-ask the model for a past effect
APPLY.commonError: Students fix the retry and forget the two messages already sent. Ask who tells the customer and how support tells a duplicate from a real second booking.
APPLY.answer: A defensible revision responds to the changed assumption, keeps missing evidence visible and names a responsible role. For the AI step, record the drafted message against the operation's key. Send only that recorded message. A retry must never ask the model again for an effect that already happened.
APPLY.sourceLabel: Course addition · not from the textbook · applies the chapter to the case

stations.concept: a retry is a new request
stations.answerKey: a second AI call is a new effect, not a check
stations.think: Devices down. What may happen on retry, and what evidence resolves the uncertainty?
stations.pair: Name one assumption and one given fact you need to support your answer.
stations.write: Write your claim and its evidence. Mark any test you only propose as proposed.
stations.hint: Name the service or property first. Use a source definition and the given facts. Ask which missing fact would change your claim. Decide what the user could receive if the retry calls the AI service again.
stations.note: Think without devices, then pair. Choosing when not to use technology is part of using it well. Use the same card; nobody is marked on field length or a timer.
stations.answer: An answer with limits separates the given facts from the needed evidence. A source explanation supports a mechanism. It does not prove the fictional deployment passed a test. Calling the AI service again is a new request, not a check on the first one. A non-deterministic model may draft a different message. That produces a second, different effect.

criteria.name: Names the mechanism
levels: Names the chapter mechanism that decides the case and says how it applies.
Names a mechanism but does not connect it to the case facts.
No chapter mechanism, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: Uses only the given facts
levels: Every statement rests on a given fact or is marked as an assumption.
Mostly given facts, but one invented or unmarked assumption.
Relies on facts the case does not give.

criteria.name: Evidence another person can check
levels: Names evidence a second engineer could inspect, and marks proposed tests as proposed.
Names evidence, but it is vague or its status is unclear.
Opinion or confidence instead of evidence.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: Claim: after the timeout the outcome is unknown; the operation may have committed. Given: the caller timed out; the trace does not show the durable effect. Proposed: a status query by operation identifier before any retry. A retry that calls the AI again may send a second, different message.
strong.why: Names the mechanism (partial failure), keeps to the given facts and proposes a checkable query.

weak.text: The server did nothing because we got no reply, so just retry.
weak.why: Treats a timeout as evidence of no execution; no check proposed.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: the key returns the recorded outcome instead of acting again
stations.think: Compare two mechanisms: a blind retry after timeout, or a retry carrying an idempotency key checked before any external effect. Which one would you choose?
stations.pair: Ask your partner to argue for the mechanism you rejected. Name one trade-off and one thing both mechanisms share.
stations.write: Write why your mechanism supports your claim, and what you are still unsure of.
stations.hint: Explain why the mechanism affects your claim. Then name a shared cause, a mismatch or a limit outside its evidence.
stations.answer: Tie the chosen mechanism to the required property. Say what the alternative improves or sacrifices. Evidence of a shared dependency or mismatched assumption can defeat an apparently stronger design. An idempotency key lets the service return the recorded outcome instead of executing again. That also stops a second, different AI-drafted message.

criteria.name: Links the mechanism to the property
levels: Explains how the chosen mechanism affects the property at stake.
Names the mechanism without the link to the property.

criteria.name: Names a shared cause or limit
levels: Names a specific shared cause, mismatch or limit that could defeat the mechanism.
Mentions a limit in general terms only.
Treats the mechanism as always enough.

criteria.name: States the trade-off
levels: Says what the alternative improves and what it costs.
Gives one side of the trade-off only.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: The idempotency key, because the property is at-most-once effect per user operation. Its limit: the key must be checked and recorded before the AI call and the send, or the window reopens. A blind retry is simpler and can double every effect.
strong.why: Links the mechanism to the property, names where it can still fail and states the trade-off.

weak.text: Retry three times; most timeouts are just slow networks.
weak.why: No property, no shared cause, treats duplicates as harmless.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

stations.answerKey: the key must be checked before the AI call and before sending
stations.think: A later trace shows that the original operation committed before its response was lost. The client's retry also called the AI service again. It drafted a different message, and both were sent. Does your first decision still hold?
stations.pair: Explain what changes in your claim, your evidence or its scope.
stations.write: Record the new evidence and your revised decision with its limits. Say plainly what your first card got wrong. Name the responsible role and who must be told.
stations.hint: Do not simply repeat your first answer. Name the changed assumption, the next evidence and the condition that would change your decision.
stations.note: Classroom version only. The assessed assignment has its own new evidence, revealed after you commit.
stations.answer: The new fact changes the stated assumption, so the original evidence cannot be widened silently. Retain, restrict or revise the decision with a reason, a new verification requirement and a named owner. The timeout hid a committed operation. The retry turned one effect into two different ones. The key must be checked before the AI call and before sending.

criteria.name: Says what the new fact changes
levels: Names the assumption the new fact breaks and what it leaves intact.
Notes the new fact without saying which assumption it breaks.
Ignores or restates the new fact.

criteria.name: Revises with a reason
levels: Keeps, changes or replaces the decision for a reason from the new fact. Says what the first answer got wrong.
Changes the decision without a clear reason, or hides the first answer.

criteria.name: Names the owner and who is told
levels: Names the role that decides and the people who must be informed.
Names neither the owner nor who is told.

rubric.marks: 2 marks per criterion, 6 in total. Not graded in class. The same reasoning earns the assignment points.

strong.text: My first card assumed no reply meant no effect; the operation had committed. Revise: check the idempotency key before the AI call and before sending, and store the first draft against it. The service owner decides; support and the affected customers are told.
strong.why: Names the broken assumption, revises with a reason, admits the first error, names owner and audience.

weak.text: Keep the retry; two messages are better than none.
weak.why: Ignores the committed operation and the duplicate effect; names nobody.

rubric.other: Other answers are accepted when they use a chapter mechanism and rest on the given facts. They must also name evidence someone else can check. A different decision with those three is as strong as the model answer.

aiAssignment.scenario: Farmers photograph diseased leaves in a mobile app. The app queues each photo while offline and sends it to a cloud AI service when connectivity returns. The service replies with a diagnosis and a recommended treatment.

criteria.name: FIT
levels: Names the chapter concept that decides the case and shows why it fits these facts.
Names the right concept, with only a partial link to the facts.
Names a concept but does not connect it to the case.
No chapter concept, or the wrong one.

criteria.name: BOUND
levels: States an observable condition that would end the claim.
Names a condition, but nobody could easily observe it.
Gives a vague limit, such as “if it fails”.

criteria.name: ACT + EVIDENCE
levels: One concrete action with an owner, and evidence another engineer could inspect even if the AI is wrong.
A concrete action, but the evidence is weak or its status is unclear.
General advice, or evidence that relies on the AI's own output.

criteria.name: REFIT
levels: Uses the new information, names the assumption it broke and justifies retain, revise or replace.
Uses the new information but does not name the broken assumption.
Keeps or changes the answer without a reason.

criteria.name: OWNER + AI USE
levels: Names the role that accepts the risk and who must be told. Declares any AI help and how it was checked.
Names a role, but not who must be told, or the AI declaration is incomplete.
Names “the team” or “the system” as owner.
No owner and no AI declaration.

rubric.marks: Practice only · not graded · score yourself 1, 0.75, 0.5 or 0 per criterion

strong.text: Each photo carries an idempotency key. The service stores the first diagnosis per key and returns it on redelivery. The design ends if one key ever gets two different diagnoses. Action: the backend lead adds the key check before the model call. Evidence: a replay test that sends 100 photos twice, proposed. After the double diagnoses I revise: the model was asked twice.
strong.why: Separates no reply from no execution, names a mechanism that stops duplicate effects, a test and an owner, and revises.

weak.text: Retry whenever there is no reply; the network is just slow.
weak.why: Treats a timeout as failure and ignores duplicates; no evidence or owner.

rubric.other: they use a chapter concept, rest on the given facts and name evidence someone else can check. A different verdict that meets these conditions is as strong as the strong example.

criteria.name: FIT
criteria.strong: The concept is partial failure with at-least-once delivery: a lost reply does not mean the diagnosis was not made. Given: intermittent connectivity; the queue redelivers; the service can take 20 seconds. Assumption, marked: the service is non-deterministic.
criteria.strongWhy: Names the chapter concept, keeps to the given facts and marks the assumption.
criteria.weak: The app just needs a better network.
criteria.weakWhy: No chapter concept; ignores the given queue guarantee.

criteria.name: FAILURE
criteria.strong: After a timeout the app knows only that no reply arrived. The photo may have been diagnosed already. A redelivery is a new request and may get a different answer.
criteria.strongWhy: Separates no reply from no execution and names the duplicate risk.
criteria.weak: If there is no reply, the service failed, so resend.
criteria.weakWhy: Treats a timeout as evidence of failure.

criteria.name: BOUND
criteria.strong: The design holds while every photo carries an idempotency key and the service returns the stored result for a repeated key. Two different diagnoses for one key reopen it.
criteria.strongWhy: Names the dependency and an observable trigger.
criteria.weak: It works unless the outage is very long.
criteria.weakWhy: No dependency and no observable trigger.

criteria.name: ACT + EVIDENCE
criteria.strong: Action: the app attaches a photo key; the service stores the first diagnosis per key and returns it on redelivery, owned by the backend lead. Evidence: a replay test that delivers 100 photos twice and shows one diagnosis each, proposed.
criteria.strongWhy: Feasible action, a named role, evidence with its status.
criteria.weakWhy: No specific action, owner or inspectable evidence.

criteria.name: REFIT
criteria.strong: The 9% double diagnoses show my design let the model answer the same photo twice. I replace the retry path: the key is checked before the model is called, and only the stored diagnosis is shown. My first plan assumed the model would answer the same way.
criteria.strongWhy: Names what changed, chooses REPLACE with a reason, admits the first assumption.
criteria.weak: I keep the design; the farmer can choose between the two treatments.
criteria.weakWhy: Pushes the duplicate onto the user; ignores the given fact.

assignmentRubric.other: the answer names the chapter concept that decides, uses only the facts given in the task, separates no reply from no execution, and names evidence from a replay test or record that someone else can check. A different design that meets these conditions earns the same marks as the model answer.
